title: Quantum Temporal Convolutional Neural Networks for Cross-Sectional Equity Return Prediction: A Comparative Benchmark Study
journal_or_venue: Preprint (submitted to IEEE Transactions on Quantum Engineering)
abstract_summary: The paper proposes QTCNN, a hybrid quantum-classical architecture that combines a classical temporal convolutional encoder with parameter-efficient quantum convolutional circuits to predict cross-sectional equity returns. The authors benchmark QTCNN on the JPX Tokyo Stock Exchange dataset, reporting improved out-of-sample Sharpe ratio (0.538) versus multiple classical and quantum baselines, and provide ablation, scalability, trainability, and noise-resilience analyses showing that both the temporal encoder and quantum entanglement contribute to the performance gains.
methodology_description: The study proposes a hybrid quantum-classical architecture named Quantum Temporal Convolutional Neural Network (QTCNN) for cross-sectional equity return prediction. The pipeline begins with the JPX (Kaggle) daily equity price dataset (2017–2022). Features are engineered per-stock: adjusted close, one-period returns, multi-scale momentum (mom{1,2,5,10,20}), rolling volatilities (vol{5,10,20}), dollar volume, rolling means and log transforms. For each trading day features are winsorized at the 1st/99th percentiles and cross-sectionally z-scored. Sequences of length seq_len=20 are built for sequence models. Labels use the competition Target (two-day holding return with one-day delay) and a weakly supervised binary labeling where the top p and bottom p stocks per day (p typically 200–300) are used as positive/negative classes; middle stocks are excluded. To reduce simulation cost a stride-based subsampling of trading days (approx. 9% of days) is applied. The QTCNN architecture: a classical temporal CNN encoder f_TConv extracts a T x F → n_q representation (global average pooling + MLP), angle-embedding (Ry rotations) maps the reduced features to n_q qubits, then a hierarchical quantum convolution + pooling circuit with intra-layer parameter sharing (6 parameters per convolutional unit) is applied. Pooling discards alternating qubits between convolutional layers, halving width each stage and constraining effective depth Leff ~ ceil(log2(n_q)). A single-qubit Pauli-Z expectation is measured and concatenated with classical features and passed through an MLP with sigmoid for binary output. Training uses binary cross-entropy, AdamW (lr=1e-3), batch sizes and epochs per model (default QTCNN: 50 epochs, batch 128). Gradients for quantum parameters are computed via the parameter-shift rule. Extensive ablations and baseline comparisons were run (classical TConv-MLP, QCNN, QNN, QLSTM, QASA, QSVM, PQC+LGBM, Transformer, LSTM, MLP, LightGBM/LambdaRank). Evaluation constructs daily cross-sectional long-short portfolios (top / bottom K=200) and uses out-of-sample annualized Sharpe ratio as the primary metric; statistical tests include paired bootstrap (B=10,000) on daily long-short returns and Ledoit–Wolf robust Sharpe testing. Additional experiments: qubit scalability (n_q in {4,6,8,10,12}), gradient variance / trainability study (200 random inits, variance of gradient of first parameter), Meyer–Wallach entanglement measure pre/post training, and noise-resilience simulations (depolarizing and amplitude-damping channels applied after each gate for p in {1e-3,5e-3,1e-2,2e-2}). Circuits were simulated in PennyLane (default.qubit / lightning.qubit and default mixed-density backend for noise), with timing measured on RTX3090 GPU + Intel i9-12900KS CPU.
algorithms_used: Variational Quantum Neural Network (QNN / circuit-centric classifier)
Classical baselines: Transformer, LSTM, MLP, LightGBM (LambdaRank)
experimental_setup: All quantum circuits were classically simulated using PennyLane (default.qubit or lightning.qubit backends). Noise-inclusive experiments used PennyLane's default mixed (density-matrix) backend inserting depolarizing and amplitude-damping channels after each gate. Primary experiments used n_q = 8 qubits (also evaluated n_q in {4,6,8,10,12}), shallow circuits (L small, effective Leff constrained by pooling), angle embedding via Ry rotations, hierarchical quantum convolution with parameter sharing (6 params per convolutional unit), pooling by discarding alternating qubits, and measurement of Pauli-Z expectations. Training used AdamW optimizer, BCE loss, parameter-shift gradients. Timing measurements reported on RTX3090 GPU + 12th Gen Intel i9-12900KS CPU.
dataset_used: JPX Tokyo Stock Exchange Prediction dataset from Kaggle (official competition dataset; training 2017–2021 with supplemental into 2022). Universe filtered to Universe0 (core ~2000 liquid stocks).

pipeline_steps: Data selection and subsampling of trading days
Feature engineering (adjusted prices, returns, momentum, volatility, volume features)
Per-day winsorization and cross-sectional z-score normalization
Labeling: top p / bottom p binary labels
Model input preparation: PCA -> angle embedding for QCNN/QNN baselines; temporal CNN encoder -> PCA/embedding for QTCNN
Quantum encoding: angle embedding via Ry rotations into n_q qubits

Quantum processing: hierarchical quantum convolutional layers with CNOT entanglement in ring topology, parameter sharing (6 params per conv unit), and pooling by discarding alternate qubits; for ablation no-CNOT variant removes entanglement
Measurement: Pauli-Z expectation(s) (single final qubit for QTCNN) concatenated with classical features
Classification head: MLP -> sigmoid; loss = binary cross-entropy
Training: gradient-based optimization using AdamW; quantum gradients via parameter-shift (2p+1 evaluations per gradient step)
Evaluation: daily cross-sectional ranking -> long-short portfolios (top/bottom K=200) -> compute daily returns and annualized Sharpe ratio on OOS period
Statistical tests: paired bootstrap (B=10,000) on daily differences, Ledoit–Wolf robust Sharpe test

Additional experiments: qubit scalability sweep n_q ∈ {4,6,8,10,12}; gradient-variance trainability study (200 random inits); entanglement measurement (Meyer–Wallach); noise simulations with depolarizing and amplitude-damping channels (p ∈ {1e-3,5e-3,1e-2,2e-2})

key_findings: [supported] The authors propose QTCNN, a hybrid quantum-classical architecture that combines a classical temporal CNN encoder with parameter-efficient quantum convolutional layers (intra-layer parameter sharing) to preserve temporal dynamics and reduce quantum parameter count.

[supported] QTCNN achieved an out-of-sample (OOS) annualized Sharpe ratio of 0.538 ± 0.042 on the JPX Tokyo Stock Exchange subset used in the study, outperforming the best classical baseline (Transformer: 0.313 ± 0.036) in these experiments (reported ~72% improvement).

[supported] The paper reports statistically significant outperformance of QTCNN vs. multiple baselines using paired bootstrap tests and a Ledoit–Wolf Sharpe test (e.g., QTCNN vs Transformer p = 0.002; QTCNN vs TConv-MLP p = 0.019; QTCNN vs QTCNN-NoEnt p = 0.038).

[supported] Ablation analysis decomposes the performance gain: temporal encoder contributed ≈ +0.099 SR, quantum single-qubit nonlinearity (no entanglement) ≈ +0.039 SR, and entanglement ≈ +0.087 SR (total QTCNN advantage over Transformer ≈ +0.225 SR).

[supported] QTCNN-NoEnt (quantum circuit with no CNOT entangling gates) still outperforms the purely classical TConv-MLP baseline, indicating single-qubit nonlinear rotations contribute representational value.

[supported] QTCNN exhibits better empirical trainability (measured gradient variance) than comparable quantum circuits without parameter sharing (QCNN and QNN): gradient variance decays approximately polynomially with qubit count for QTCNN, while QCNN and QNN show near-exponential decay consistent with barren-plateau behavior.

[supported] Qubit scalability study: QTCNN Sharpe improves from nq=4 to nq≈10 (peak around nq=10 at SR≈0.551) and shows a slight decline at nq=12 (SR≈0.529), consistent with increasing training difficulty at larger qubit counts.

[supported] Simulated noise experiments: QTCNN maintains performance above the best classical baseline up to depolarizing two-qubit error rates on the order of p≈0.01; at near-term representative error rates (p≈1e-3) performance degrades only slightly in simulation.

[supported] The authors do not claim a computational (algorithmic) quantum speedup; they interpret observed gains as representational (inductive-bias) advantages of the quantum feature map/variational circuit.

[speculative] The paper attributes QTCNN's improvement to quantum mechanisms such as Hilbert-space expressibility, entanglement-enabled feature interactions, and quantum interference acting as implicit feature selection / regularization.

[speculative] Authors argue the parameter-sharing design mitigates barren-plateau effects and that QTCNN may remain trainable up to ≈20 qubits (extrapolated), but this is an extrapolation beyond empirically simulated qubit counts.

[speculative] The authors suggest QTCNN could be feasible on near-term NISQ hardware given sufficient two-qubit gate fidelity (they mention fidelity targets ≳99%), and that error mitigation (ZNE/PEC) could further help—this is a projection based on simulated noise models rather than hardware runs.

[speculative] The paper notes dequantization caveats: while no computational speedup is claimed and state-vector simulation is possible at the reported scales, the angle-embedding approach used is argued to be outside the class of encodings targeted by some dequantization results—but full dequantization risk at larger scales remains an open question.

[supported] In the experimental setup used, the top-performing models in this benchmark were quantum-based (QTCNN, QNN, QTCNN-NoEnt) and the temporal encoder (classical) was an important component; pure classical LSTM performed poorly on this small OOS evaluation.

[speculative] Hardware resource and fault-tolerant scaling statements (e.g., an estimate that 16 logical qubits would require ~16,000 physical qubits under surface code at a certain physical error rate) are presented as roadmap-level projections rather than demonstrated deployments.
results_summary: The preprint proposes QTCNN, a hybrid model that pairs a classical temporal CNN encoder with a parameter-shared quantum convolutional network. In simulations on a subsampled JPX dataset, QTCNN produced the highest reported out-of-sample Sharpe (0.538 ±0.042) among the compared baselines, with ablations indicating that both the temporal encoder and quantum components (single-qubit nonlinearities and entanglement) contribute to the gain. The authors present statistical tests, qubit-scaling experiments, gradient-variance (trainability) analyses, and noisy-circuit simulations, concluding that QTCNN provides a representational (not computational) advantage in this controlled benchmark, while acknowledging dataset, subsampling, and simulation limitations.
performance_claims: QTCNN OOS Sharpe ratio 0.538 ± 0.042 (22 OOS days, 5 runs).
Reported relative improvement of QTCNN over best classical baseline ≈ 72% (0.538 vs 0.313).
Ablation decomposition: temporal encoder +0.099 SR, quantum nonlinearity +0.039 SR, entanglement +0.087 SR (sum ≈ +0.225 SR over Transformer).
QTCNN remains above the best classical baseline in simulated depolarizing noise up to p ≈ 0.01; at p = 10^-3 degradation is small (~3.2% in the reported simulation).
Qubit scalability: QTCNN Sharpe by nq — 4: 0.347±0.058; 6: 0.461±0.049; 8: 0.538±0.042; 10: 0.551±0.047; 12: 0.529±0.055 (simulation results reported).
Gradient variance measurements show QTCNN decays approximately polynomially with nq (empirical fit) while QCNN/QNN show more rapid (near-exponential) decay consistent with barren-plateau behavior.
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors present empirical evidence (simulated) of improved risk-adjusted returns (Sharpe) for their QTCNN model in a constrained benchmark and attribute gains to representational properties (Hilbert-space embedding, entanglement, implicit regularization). However, the experiments use classical state-vector simulation at small qubit counts, a heavily subsampled dataset with a short OOS period (22 days), and simulated noise models. The paper does not claim algorithmic computational speedup, and extrapolations to larger qubit counts or hardware are conjectural; therefore the claim of a practical quantum advantage is speculative pending larger-scale evaluation and real-device validation.
limitations: Computational constraints requiring aggressive subsampling of trading days (stride-based sampling) that reduced training data and forced a small out-of-sample (OOS) evaluation window (22 days)
Limited statistical power of the OOS evaluation (22 days) that constrains reliability of Sharpe-ratio comparisons and effect-size estimates
Noise modeling in experiments is limited to depolarizing and amplitude-damping channels; device-specific noise sources (crosstalk, readout errors, non-Markovian effects) were not characterized
All quantum circuits were classically simulated (state-vector / density-matrix backends); simulation overhead and artifacts do not reflect true quantum-hardware performance
No claim of computational quantum speedup in the small-qubit (nq ≤ 8) simulation regime — results are representational rather than computational
Modeling choices and dataset limitations: experiments focused on JPX Kaggle dataset (2017–2022) and Universe0 stocks only, which may limit coverage of market regimes and generalizability
Use of weak supervision (training on top/bottom p stocks per day and excluding middle-range stocks) may introduce a distribution mismatch between training and full-universe inference
Limited feature set and preprocessing choices: sector codes were not used in main models and feature engineering focused on price/volume technical indicators only
Evaluation excludes market frictions: transaction costs, bid-ask spreads, slippage, and market impact were not modeled
Small scale of quantum circuits (primarily nq = 8) limits conclusions about behavior at larger qubit counts and about practical hardware resource demands
Limited number of independent experimental runs (reported 5 runs for OOS Sharpe reporting) which may understate model variance across seeds and retrainings

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — QTCNN (hybrid temporal CNN + parameter-efficient quantum convolutional circuits) attains higher out-of-sample annualized Sharpe (0.538) versus multiple classical and quantum baselines on the JPX Kaggle dataset (long-short top/bottom K portfolios).

#idea:hybrid-approach — Classical temporal convolutional encoder reduces feature dimensionality before angle-embedding into n_q qubits, enabling a parameter-efficient quantum convolution + pooling pipeline and practical hybrid training (parameter-shift gradients + AdamW).

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Design choices (hierarchical pooling that halves qubits per stage, parameter sharing with 6 params/unit, shallow circuits, n_q in {4,6,8,10,12}) are motivated for NISQ-era deployment and the authors report noise-resilience simulations.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Ablation studies attribute performance gains to both the temporal encoder and quantum entanglement (Meyer–Wallach entanglement measure increases post-training), suggesting a non-trivial role of quantum circuit structure in ranking performance.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Benchmarks include many baselines (Transformer, LSTM, MLP, LightGBM/LambdaRank, QCNN, QNN, QLSTM, QASA, QSVM, PQC+LGBM) with paired bootstrap and Ledoit–Wolf Sharpe tests to assess statistical significance of observed improvements.

#limitation:simulation-only — All quantum experiments were run on classical simulators (PennyLane default.qubit / lightning.qubit and mixed-density backend for noise); no real-QPU experiments are reported.

#limitation:qubit-count — Scalability tested only up to 12 qubits with aggressive pooling; primary reported experiments use n_q = 8, limiting evidence for scaling to larger, production-grade universes.

#limitation:noise — Noise resilience is evaluated via simulated depolarizing and amplitude-damping channels with error rates p in {1e-3,5e-3,1e-2,2e-2}, but real-device noise characteristics and error mitigation are not demonstrated on hardware.

#limitation:data-encoding — Angle (Ry) embedding and aggressive dimensionality reduction (temporal encoder / pooling) are used to fit features into few qubits; the cost and fidelity of realistic data-loading on hardware remain untested.

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — Dataset processing includes heavy stride-based subsampling (~9% of days) to reduce computation, producing small training/OOS day counts (~100 training days, ~22 OOS days) which constrains claims of out-of-sample generality in live trading settings.
contradictions: The paper asserts near-term feasibility and reports a quantum-driven performance uplift, but all results are from classical simulation with heavy temporal subsampling and small qubit counts (<=12). This raises a scalability contradiction: the evidence does not demonstrate that the claimed improvements would hold on real QPUs or scale to full-market, continuously-sampled training (contradiction:scalability).
